$n=312=2^3\cdot3\cdot13$: divisors $1,2,3,4,6,8,12,13,24,26,39,52,78,104,156,312$, so $d_8=13$. Then $d_j^2-d_i^2=169=1\cdot169$, giving $(d_i,d_j)=(84,85)$, neither a divisor.

Remaining $n<360$ with $\tau(n)\ge9$ are $315,320,324,330,336,340,342,348,350,352$. In each case either $d_8^2$ admits no factorisation $uv$ with $u,v$ of the same parity yielding divisor pairs, or the resulting $(d_i,d_j)$ are not divisors of $n$. (Numbers with exactly $8$ divisors are impossible, since then $d_8=n$ forces $d_j>n$.)

For $n<360$ we must have $d_8\ge9$, because $d_8\le8$ would require $1,2,\dots,7\mid n$, i.e. $n\ge\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,7)=420>360$.

If $d_8=9$, then $d_j^2-d_i^2=81$, so $(d_i,d_j)\in\{(12,15),(40,41)\}$. The pair $(40,41)$ forces $n\ge\operatorname{lcm}(9,40,41)=14760$. The pair $(12,15)$ forces $180\mid n$. The only multiples of $180$ below $360$ are $180$ itself, but $180$ has divisors $1,2,3,4,5,6,9,10,\dots$, giving $d_8=10\neq9$.

Finally $n=360=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5$ has divisors
$$1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12,15,18,20,24,30,36,40,45,60,72,90,120,180,360,$$
so $d_8=9$, and
$$9^2+12^2=81+144=225=15^2,$$
with $12=d_{10}$ and $15=d_{11}$ both divisors of $360$.

\boxed{360}
